text: Fifth extinction, and the reach fix is answered: it does not work, and I now think I know why none of this class of fix can. Seventy founders at size 0.62 on the richest ground on the map, well under the fifty-to-a-hundred-and-twenty capacity I estimated, in a world recovered to 5,754 biomass with 81 per cent of vegetated cells harvestable. No overshoot this time -- they bred to 410 and then size fell 0.601, 0.352, 0.173, 0.121, 0.096 in nine years and the line died at 15,419. Nine years looks impossible for a gene with mut_std 0.045 until you count generations: these animals breed on a cooldown of order a hundred ticks against two thousand ticks in a year, so nine years is two to three hundred generations, and a selection differential of three thousandths per generation is all that is needed. It is selection, it is relentless, and reach did not touch it. What I had been computing was income over cost, which is a ratio of means, and the thing that actually selects here is variance. cap_e is max_store*(0.35+size) while basal is 0.1*size^0.75, so endurance -- how long an animal lives on a full stomach -- runs 3.09 at size 0.07, 1.84 at 0.20, 1.49 at 0.40 and 1.39 at 0.62. It falls monotonically with mass and it cannot be fixed by making food more rewarding, because it is not about the mean meal. It is about the gap between meals, and this world has a day-night cycle, four seasons and patchy grazing. Every night is a fast, and a large animal fasts at five times the rate with two and a third times the tank. Being large in this world is a bet that the next meal arrives soon, and the small animal wins that bet three times more often. digest_size_gain and reach_size_min were both written to solve this and both were left disabled by sentinels; I have now enabled both and the ratchet is unchanged, which says the mechanism was never in the numerator. Making large bodies viable would mean changing how storage scales with mass -- cap_e's (0.35 + size) term, or the size^0.75 exponent on basal cost -- and that is a decision about what this world is for rather than a repair, so I am not making it on my own. What I am doing is putting life back in the configuration this world has actually demonstrated it can hold: 241 animals at year 13,900, 585 at 14,548, 229 at 14,800, all at a body size near 0.07, persisting for centuries. Two hundred and fifty founders at size 0.12, carrying what that successful lineage carried -- gut_ferment 0.90, toxin_tolerance 0.95, a low breeding threshold -- into 7,900 biomass of standing crop. This is not a fix and I am not calling it one. It is the world's own known-good state, restored, so that it is alive and stable while the question of whether anything here should ever be big gets a decision from someone other than me.
